asset: Aldergate · T1 Transformer · Autotransformer · Bushing Set
signal: Aldergate T1 345 kV bushing C1 power factor still climbing
aiInterpretation: C1 power factor on the A-phase 345 kV bushing has risen from 0.376 % at 09:30 to 0.956 %, with capacitance deviation and leakage current moving with it. Three independent bushing measurements trending together points at the condenser core, not the instrument.

detail.signal: C1 power factor 0.956 % against a 0.376 % baseline at 09:30 — it doubled at 12:30 and is still rising. Capacitance deviation is up from 0.50 % to 4.19 % and leakage current from 43.4 mA to 59.7 mA.
detail.observed: C1 power factor, capacitance deviation and leakage current on the A-phase 345 kV bushing are all rising monotonically since 09:30. B and C phase bushings are flat. Top oil 64.6 °C, normal for the load, and T1 is only at 68 % of nameplate.
detail.derived: Power factor has doubled from this bushing’s own baseline, which is the published trigger for closer monitoring; a tripling is the trigger to remove from service. Capacitance deviation is still under the 5 % investigate threshold but rising faster than power factor, which is the order you expect when grading layers short.
detail.inferred: Moisture ingress or partial discharge shorting grading layers in the condenser core. Shorted layers raise capacitance, which is what the deviation trend shows.
detail.recommendation: Doble power factor and capacitance test at the next outage window, corrected to 20 °C and compared against nameplate and the sister phases. Treat monitored evolution as unpredictable: documented cases run from ten days of warning down to minutes.

relatedOccurrences.summary: Wyndham T1 C-phase bushing replaced after a similar power factor trend; core found wet at teardown.

detail.whatChangedSummary: Bushing monitor alerts at 09:30 and 12:30; no switching or load change on T1.

whatChanged.description: Bushing monitor first-stage alert on A-phase C1 power factor
Second-stage alert: power factor doubled from baseline
Doble test added to the Saturday outage request

detail.risk: High — bushing failure takes the transformer and can damage adjacent plant
detail.expectedOutcome: Power factor continues to rise until the bushing is replaced.

asset: Kessler · T2 Transformer · Autotransformer · DGA Monitor
signal: Kessler T2 combustible gas rate creeping up
aiInterpretation: TDCG rate of change has climbed from 1.77 ppm/day at 08:10 to 9.02 ppm/day, with ethylene and hydrogen rising together and acetylene flat. That gas pattern is thermal, not arcing.

detail.signal: TDCG rate 9.02 ppm/day against 1.77 ppm/day this morning. Ethylene 41.6 ppm (from 13.9), hydrogen 90.0 ppm (from 31.7), total combustible gas 363.1 ppm, acetylene unchanged at 0.27 ppm.
detail.observed: Ethylene, hydrogen and total combustible gas all rising through the shift on T2 only. Acetylene flat. T2 load and winding temperature are normal for the day, and T1 next to it shows nothing.
detail.derived: Rising methane, ethane and ethylene with no acetylene is the published thermal-fault signature. The rate is still well below the 30 ppm/day action level, so this is a trend to track rather than a reason to remove the bank.
detail.inferred: A developing local hot spot — a loose joint or a blocked oil duct is the usual cause at this gas pattern. Not yet confirmed.
detail.recommendation: Resample from the main tank within 24 hours and confirm the rate rather than the absolute values. Run Duval triangle on the confirmed sample. Keep T2 loaded normally meanwhile.
detail.whatChangedSummary: No switching, no load change on T2 — the gas trend is the only thing that moved.

whatChanged.description: Online DGA monitor rate-of-change advisory on T2
Infrared scan of T2 bushings and leads found nothing external

detail.confidence: Single online monitor, not yet confirmed by lab sample
detail.risk: Medium — slow-evolving, but the gas pattern is unambiguous
detail.expectedOutcome: Lab resample confirms or clears the rate before end of week.

signal: Larkspur 138 kV bus CVT reading low — nothing else agrees
aiInterpretation: The A-phase bus CVT drifted 6.12 % away from the redundant relay measurement with no corresponding movement in MW, MVAr, line current or the adjacent bus. A real voltage change moves every measurement together; this one moved alone.

detail.signal: Redundant measurement deviation 6.12 %, past the 5 % alarm threshold at 11:35, while angle deviation stayed under 2°. Secondary voltage fell from 68.01 V to 63.80 V over the same window.
detail.observed: One CVT secondary drifting down since 09:00. The redundant relay on the same bus, the Wyndham–Larkspur line CVT, the 138 kV MW and MVAr flows and the 69 kV bus voltage are all unchanged.
detail.derived: Magnitude deviation above 0.05 pu between two relays on the same bus, with angle deviation under the 10° threshold, is the published instrument-fault signature rather than a system event.
detail.inferred: Capacitor elements shorting in the CVT stack, which lowers the ratio. Moisture in the stack gives the same signature.
detail.recommendation: Automatic voltage control using this CVT was blocked at 12:10 so the tap changer stops chasing a voltage that was never wrong. Replace the CVT at the next clearance; offline capacitance should be within 1–2 % of nameplate.

relatedOccurrences.summary: Kessler 345 kV line CVT replaced for the same slow ratio drift.

detail.whatChangedSummary: Auto voltage control blocked on this input at 12:10; the drift stopped mattering.

whatChanged.description: Redundant measurement deviation advisory raised
Deviation crossed the 5 % alarm threshold
Blocked Larkspur bus CVT as a voltage control source

detail.risk: Low — caught before the voltage control scheme acted on it
detail.expectedOutcome: Bus voltage regulation unaffected; CVT replaced at the next clearance.

asset: Wyndham · T1 Transformer · Autotransformer · Tap Changer
aiInterpretation: Tap operations per day jumped from 4.6 to a peak of 57.5 after 09:50, with the tap oscillating either side of its normal position and no net drift, and it held there for three hours. Regulated voltage never left its band, so nothing looked wrong on the voltage gauge — the wear was the whole story.

detail.signal: Tap operations per day peaked at 57.5 against a normal 4.6, with tap position cycling ±2 steps. Since the bandwidth change at 12:45 the rate is back to 13.0 ops/day.
detail.observed: Tap position oscillating ±2 steps with no net direction from 09:50. Regulated 138 kV bus voltage stayed inside band throughout. The paralleled Aldergate T1 was tapping in counter-phase over the same window.
detail.derived: Bandwidth was set at 1.5 V against a 0.75 V per step regulator — less than the two steps required to prevent hunting. At the peak rate this bank would consume its 50,000–100,000 operation maintenance interval years early.
detail.inferred: Control bandwidth too narrow, aggravated by the parallel bank fighting it.
detail.recommendation: Bandwidth widened to 2.0 V at 12:45 and the time delay lengthened to 30 s. Review the paralleling scheme and the line-drop compensation settings before the next hot spell.

relatedOccurrences.summary: Same bank hunted for two days after a paralleling scheme change; settings were reverted.

detail.whatChangedSummary: Bandwidth widened from 1.5 V to 2.0 V and the time delay set to 30 s at 12:45.

whatChanged.description: Tap operation rate advisory on T1
Operation rate settled near 57/day
Voltage regulator bandwidth 1.5 V → 2.0 V, delay 20 s → 30 s

detail.confidence: Confirmed by tap position and bandwidth review
detail.risk: Medium — no operational risk, but contact wear was accumulating fast
detail.expectedOutcome: Operation rate settles near 12–15/day over the next few hours.

signal: Orrin–Larkspur 138 kV locked out after a failed reclose
aiInterpretation: A single-phase-to-ground fault at 10:15 tripped both ends. The one reclose attempt failed and the lockout relay operated, so the circuit is out of service and out of the contingency set. Line patrol is en route.

detail.signal: Flow went from 56.2 MW to zero in one scan at 10:15. The breaker operations counter stepped by 2, the reclose counter by 1, and accumulated interrupted energy by 3.84 kA²s.
detail.observed: Both ends open and locked out since 10:20. Every 138 kV bus registered a voltage dip in the same scan — 0.063 pu at Orrin, 0.058 pu at Larkspur, 0.018 pu at Aldergate — and all recovered on fault clearing.
detail.derived: Sag depth falls off with electrical distance from the fault and every bus saw it simultaneously, which is consistent with a fault on this circuit rather than a local problem at either station.
detail.inferred: A permanent fault. Most transmission faults are temporary and clear on the first reclose; this one did not, so there is something physically on the line.
detail.recommendation: Patrol between structures 41 and 78 first, where the fault locator puts it. Hold the restricted configuration until the circuit is back: the binding contingency is now the Wyndham–Larkspur circuit, not this one.

relatedOccurrences.summary: Same circuit tripped and reclosed successfully during a storm cell.

detail.whatChangedSummary: Circuit tripped, reclosed unsuccessfully and locked out; configuration restricted since.

whatChanged.description: A-phase to ground fault, both ends tripped
Reclose attempt unsuccessful — 86 lockout operated
Restricted configuration declared for Harrow District
Line patrol dispatched to structures 41–78

detail.confidence: Confirmed by relay event report and fault locator
detail.risk: High — the network is running on one path where it had two
detail.expectedOutcome: Circuit restored once the patrol finds and clears the cause.

signal: Larkspur exposed on the next contingency
aiInterpretation: With Orrin–Larkspur out, the flow it carried is arriving the long way round. Larkspur’s worst post-contingency loading crossed 100 % of emergency rating at 10:35 and peaked at 105.1 % at 11:20. Closing the Navarre–Dunmore tie pulled it back under, but the margin is gone.

detail.signal: Worst N-1 post-contingency loading peaked at 105.1 % of emergency rating at 11:20 and is 98.6 % now. Pre-contingency loading peaked at 86.0 % — nothing is actually overloaded.
detail.observed: Wyndham–Larkspur went from 105.5 MW to 140.7 MW and Larkspur–Wexford from 30.5 MW to 48.1 MW within three scans of the lockout. Larkspur T1 rose from 36.0 MVA to 61.9 MVA. Closing the 69 kV tie at 11:20 moved 11.2 MW to Navarre and took T1 back to 51.7 MVA.
detail.derived: The binding contingency is now loss of Wyndham–Larkspur, which would put Larkspur T1 and the Larkspur–Wexford circuit above their emergency ratings. Closing the tie transferred load but also put 8.1 MVA onto Bexhill T1, whose own worst case is now 97.3 % — the exposure moved rather than disappearing.
detail.inferred: This is redistribution, not a fault: flow divides by impedance, and the 138 kV network was never sized to carry what the lost circuit was carrying.
detail.recommendation: Hold the restricted configuration and keep the tie closed until Orrin–Larkspur is back. Defer any switching in Harrow District that would take a second element out. Watch Bexhill T1, which is now the second most exposed element.

relatedOccurrences.summary: Same circuit out for planned work; the tie was closed then too, with the same transfer to Bexhill.

detail.whatChangedSummary: Tie closed at 11:20 to relieve Larkspur T1; exposure partly transferred to Bexhill.

whatChanged.description: Orrin–Larkspur 138 kV lockout — flow redistributed
Worst post-contingency loading crossed 100 % of emergency rating

Bexhill T1 loading up 8.1 MVA as a result of the transfer

detail.confidence: Confirmed by contingency analysis and measured flows
detail.risk: High — no margin for a second element loss in Harrow District
detail.expectedOutcome: Margin returns when Orrin–Larkspur is restored.

signal: Dunmore 69 kV bus voltage sagged — cause was two stations away
aiInterpretation: Dunmore’s 69 kV bus fell to 0.943 pu, below the 0.95 pu pre-contingency floor. Nothing at Dunmore changed: the Wyndham 138 kV capacitor bank tripped on neutral unbalance at 09:40, and Dunmore is the electrically weakest point behind it.

detail.signal: Bus voltage 1.007 pu → 0.943 pu at its lowest, against a 0.95 pu pre-contingency floor. Recovered to 0.977 pu after the tap change at 10:35 and is 0.984 pu now.
detail.observed: Wyndham capacitor bank neutral unbalance current stepped from 0.144 A to 1.314 A at 09:40 and stayed there; the bank went out in the same scan. Dunmore sagged 0.064 pu, Larkspur 69 kV 0.044 pu, and Wyndham’s own 138 kV bus only 0.018 pu.
detail.derived: The deepest sag is furthest from the cause, which is normal for a reactive loss: voltage falls where the network is weakest, not where the equipment failed. A step in neutral unbalance that does not return is a failed capacitor can and its fuse, not a measurement drift.
detail.inferred: One capacitor can failed and its fuse operated, unbalancing the bank enough to trip it. The next failure in the same phase group will come sooner than this one did.
detail.recommendation: Larkspur and Colvin taps were raised two steps at 10:35 as the interim fix. Inspect the bank, find the failed can, and re-baseline the inherent unbalance before returning it. Until then Wyndham and Thorne are short of reactive reserve.

relatedOccurrences.summary: Same bank lost a can; the unbalance step was about the same size.

detail.whatChangedSummary: Wyndham capacitor bank tripped on neutral unbalance; taps raised to recover 69 kV voltage.

whatChanged.description: Wyndham 138 kV capacitor bank tripped on neutral unbalance
Dunmore 69 kV undervoltage advisory

detail.confidence: Confirmed by the timing of the unbalance step
detail.risk: Low — voltage recovered, but the bank is out and reserve is thin
detail.expectedOutcome: Voltage holds with the raised taps until the bank is repaired.

asset: Wexford · Tilbury 69 kV Line · Circuit Breaker
signal: Five momentary faults on Wexford–Tilbury 69 kV this shift
aiInterpretation: The circuit auto-reclosed successfully five times between 08:25 and 12:00. No customer was interrupted and no single event was worth an alarm, but the pattern is well above this circuit’s normal rate and the breaker has been accumulating wear.

detail.signal: Reclose counter 10 against 5 at the start of shift — events at 08:25, 09:15, 10:05, 11:10 and 12:00. Accumulated interrupted energy is up 2.10 kA²s and contact wear up 1.8 points over the same period.
detail.observed: Each event is a successful reclose within a second; Tilbury 69 kV registered a 0.043 pu dip at each one and Wexford 0.028 pu. Nothing since the 12:20 patrol.
detail.derived: Five momentaries in under four hours against a normal rate of about one a week. Momentary outages last under a minute by definition, which is why none of them reached the outage log.
detail.inferred: Something intermittent on the line — vegetation or wildlife. Repeated temporary faults on one circuit usually become a permanent one.
detail.recommendation: The patrol found and cleared a limb contacting the B phase near structure 22 at 12:20. Keep the circuit on watch to end of shift and raise a vegetation work order for the span.

relatedOccurrences.summary: Same span produced three momentaries before a limb was removed.

signal: Kessler T1 winding hot spot climbing on the afternoon ramp
aiInterpretation: Hot spot rose from 73.7 °C at 10:20 to 107.9 °C at 12:50 as ambient and load climbed together. All twelve fans were already running, and T1 was carrying 54 MVA more than T2 — the two banks were not sharing the extra load evenly.

detail.signal: Winding hot spot 73.7 °C → 107.9 °C between 10:20 and 12:50, past the 105 °C alert at 12:35 and against a 110 °C continuous limit for a 65 °C rise unit. Loading peaked at 93.9 % of nameplate with ambient at 32.1 °C. It is 99.4 °C now.
detail.observed: All cooling stages ran from the start of the ramp and top oil followed the hot spot at the expected gradient, so the cooling was working — there simply was not any more of it. T1 was at 140.8 MVA against T2’s 87.1 MVA at 12:45 on identical 150 MVA banks.
detail.derived: Hot spot tracked the value calculated from load and ambient within 2 °C throughout, which rules out a cooling fault and confirms genuine overload. Aging roughly doubles for every 6 °C above the design point, so the excursion costs real life even though nothing tripped.
detail.inferred: Load plus ambient, made worse by unequal sharing between the paralleled banks. The redistributed flow after the Orrin–Larkspur lockout put more through Kessler than the day would otherwise have done, and the tap mismatch sent most of it to T1.
detail.recommendation: Taps were rebalanced at 12:50 and both banks now sit near 116.6 MVA, with the hot spot back under 100 °C. Keep them matched until ambient drops, and check the paralleling settings before the morning ramp rather than during it.

relatedOccurrences.summary: T1 reached 106 °C on the July peak day; same mitigation used.

detail.whatChangedSummary: Tap positions rebalanced at 12:50; the banks now share evenly and the hot spot is falling.

whatChanged.description: Load and hot spot rise began with the redistribution

detail.confidence: Confirmed against the calculated hot spot
detail.risk: Medium — brief excursion, small loss of life, no damage
detail.expectedOutcome: Hot spot stays below 100 °C through the evening peak with the banks matched.

signal: Thorne reactive reserve nearly gone while MW flows look comfortable
aiInterpretation: Thorne’s 345 kV circuits are at 57 % and 34 % of normal rating and nothing on the MW display looks wrong. The reactive reserve behind those flows has fallen from 168.5 MVAr to 38.2 MVAr — the Wyndham bank is out and the shunt reactor is now committed.

detail.signal: Reactive reserve 38.2 MVAr against a 120 MVAr operating target and 168.5 MVAr this morning. It stepped down 52 MVAr when the Wyndham bank tripped at 09:40 and slid a further 73 MVAr between 11:10 and 11:40. MW loading is unchanged.
detail.observed: Wyndham’s 50 MVAr capacitor bank has been out since 09:40, taking Wyndham’s own reserve from 161.2 MVAr to 109.9 MVAr as well. Thorne’s switchable reactive fell a further 41 MVAr as the reactor was committed to holding 345 kV voltage through the ramp.
detail.derived: Real power headroom and reactive headroom are not the same headroom. The loading percentage everyone watches says there is plenty of room; the reactive reserve says the next voltage event has almost nothing left to answer it with.
detail.inferred: Not a fault. The reserve was consumed by the capacitor bank outage and the afternoon ramp, and no single display shows both halves of it.
detail.recommendation: Restore the Wyndham bank as the first priority — it is worth more here than any redispatch. Until then, treat a voltage event in Keldon or Harrow as unbacked, and pre-position the Thorne reactor out of service rather than in.
detail.whatChangedSummary: Capacitor bank outage plus the afternoon ramp consumed the reserve; MW flows unchanged.

detail.risk: Medium — nothing is wrong now, and little is available if it goes wrong
detail.expectedOutcome: Reserve recovers when the Wyndham bank returns.

signal: Colvin 69 kV voltage distortion drifting toward the limit
aiInterpretation: Total harmonic distortion on the Colvin 69 kV bus has drifted from 0.97 % to 2.05 % through the day while voltage, flows and every equipment temperature stayed normal. The IEEE 519 limit for this voltage class is 2.5 %.

detail.signal: Bus THD 2.05 % against a 2.5 % limit for 69 kV, up from 0.97 % at 09:05. Negative sequence voltage has risen 0.43 points over the same window, and Tilbury one circuit away is up 0.56 points.
detail.observed: Distortion rising steadily at Colvin and, more weakly, at Tilbury. Bus voltage, MW and MVAr flows and transformer temperatures are all normal.
detail.derived: The rise tracks the load ramp, and the distortion is worse closer to Colvin, so the source is downstream of Colvin rather than on the 138 kV system.
detail.inferred: A customer drive load that has come on and is running without its filter bank. Not confirmed with the customer yet.
detail.recommendation: Put a power quality recorder on the Colvin 69 kV bus before the evening peak and contact the customer about filter status. If it reaches 2.5 % the limit is absolute regardless of who caused it.

signal: Bexhill T1 relay test clearance cannot be taken today
aiInterpretation: The Bexhill T1 protection test is due on 31 August under its six-year interval and needs four hours. With Orrin–Larkspur still out, taking T1 out of service would put Harrow District above 100 % post contingency — and there are under four hours of switching window left.

detail.signal: District worst post-contingency loading 98.6 % with T1 in service. The study with T1 out returns 118 % on the Bexhill–Orrin circuit. Time needed 4h 00m; time left in the switching window 3h 55m.
detail.observed: The clearance request was reviewed at 13:40 and the contingency study run at 13:50. Both the margin and the clock fail.
detail.derived: Time needed exceeds time left even before the contingency result, so this is a scheduling problem first and a reliability problem second. The compliance date is still three days out.
detail.inferred: Not an equipment problem at all — a plan that assumed the network would be intact.
detail.recommendation: Defer the clearance to Saturday and pair it with the Aldergate T1 bushing Doble test, which needs the same crew. If Orrin–Larkspur is not back by Friday, escalate the compliance date rather than taking the element out.
